answers.text:
Computational functionalism is the philosophical position that Seth identifies as the hidden load-bearing assumption behind the whole idea of conscious AI: the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation — more specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. Seth stresses that this isn't a proven fact but a premise people take for granted: this assumption... is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all. But that is what it is.

Why it matters here: this term names the target of the entire section that follows ("Consciousness & Computation"). Seth is about to spend four arguments (brains-aren't-computers, other-games-in-town, life-matters, simulation-isn't-instantiation) trying to knock this assumption down. His stakes are explicit: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with.

Later in the essay he sharpens the distinction between this specific claim and a broader, more defensible one: functionalism: the idea that properties of mind (including consciousness) depend on the functional organization of the (embodied) brain is a looser position that many philosophers hold, whereas computational functionalism... implies that the type of organization that matters is computational and which in turn is often assumed to relate to Turing-style algorithms in particular — the narrower, stronger claim that Seth is actually arguing against. In short: it's the view that if you run the right program, consciousness just happens — no biology, no body, no life required — and it's the assumption that has to be true for anything like ChatGPT or a whole-brain simulation to ever actually feel like something from the inside.

answers.asked: This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all.
answers.text:
This sentence names the assumption Seth is about to spend the rest of the essay dismantling: computational functionalism, the view — stated in the sentence just before this one — that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. His point here is not about the content of the assumption but about its invisibility: because so much of modern thinking about minds and machines already treats the brain as a kind of computer, people rarely notice that "consciousness = the right computation" is a substantive philosophical claim at all — it functions more like unquestioned background common sense than like a position that could be argued for or against.

That's the rhetorical hinge of this section. Having flagged the assumption as usually invisible, Seth immediately commits to treating it as an assumption rather than a fact: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with. Everything that follows — the four arguments about brains not being computers, other non-Turing "games in town," biological naturalism, and the simulation/instantiation distinction — is Seth's attempt to pry this assumption loose from the status of obvious truth and hold it up for scrutiny.

answers.asked: What does "computational functionalism" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, computational functionalism is the assumption that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise, and Seth notes that this assumption... is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all [spya-wepmnr]. Later he sharpens the definition further, calling it the claim that (algorithmic) computation is sufficient for consciousness [spya-ymbpwn], and distinguishes it from the more general philosophical position of functionalism — the idea that mental properties depend on a system's functional organization — noting that computational functionalism is the narrower, specific claim that this organization must be computational, typically in the Turing-machine sense [spya-f0qxnb].

Why it matters: it is the load-bearing premise under the whole idea of conscious AI. Seth says outright that the very idea of conscious AI rests on the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation... And if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with [spya-wepmnr]. The bulk of the essay's central section — the four arguments about brains not being computers, other non-computational "games in town," life mattering, and simulation not being instantiation — is aimed at showing this assumption is shakier than it looks. He sums up that computational functionalism... is a very strong assumption that looks increasingly shaky as the many and deep differences between brains and (standard digital) computers come into view [spya-ymbpwn]. He also flags it as a kind of quiet default among rival theories: These theories generally avoid proposing sufficient conditions for consciousness. They also generally sidestep defending computational functionalism, being content instead to assume it [spya-qu7j89] — which is part of why he thinks the assumption needs to be surfaced and argued against rather than left implicit.

My inference is that this is the pivot of the whole essay's structure: everything before it (the section on psychological biases) explains why people are inclined to *believe* in conscious AI without examining this premise, and everything after it builds the ethical argument on the conclusion that the premise is doubtful.

The article glosses the word itself a few lines later: "This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for 'self-production.' Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems." So in context here, it names the fact that a single neuron isn't just passively computing but is constantly rebuilding the physical stuff it's made of, using its own activity to keep itself in existence.

The term itself comes from outside the article: it was coined in the 1970s by the biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to define what makes something alive. As one source summarizes, the theory was introduced as an attempt to describe the abstract logical organisation of the cell and provide an essentialist definition of life. The core idea is that a living system is one whose parts are continually producing and regenerating the very network that produces them, so that the organism is, in effect, the ongoing process of making itself. One formal statement of it: "An autopoietic system is organized as a network of processes of production of components which: (a) through their transformations and interactions continuously regenerate the network of processes that produced them, and (b) constitute the system as a concrete unity in the space in which it exists." Maturana and Varela went further and treated this as the dividing line between the living and the non-living: "Autopoiesis in the physical space is a necessary and sufficient condition for a system to be a living one."

Seth is leaning on that pedigree to make a specific move in his argument: a computer chip doesn't rebuild its own transistors to stay in existence, but a neuron does something like this constantly, at the molecular level, just to remain a neuron. That difference — self-maintenance versus a fixed, externally-manufactured substrate — is one plank in his case that brains are not simply "meat computers," and later in the essay it becomes part of his suggestion that being alive in this self-producing sense may be part of what consciousness requires, not just running the right software.

answers.asked: (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for “self-production.” Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)
answers.text:
Autopoiesis is a concept from biology and systems theory, most closely associated with the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, who coined it in the early 1970s to describe how living systems continuously produce and maintain themselves. A cell, for instance, doesn't just sit there being a cell — it's constantly rebuilding its own components, repairing its membrane, replacing molecules that break down, using its own processes to regenerate the very conditions that let it keep existing. The term literally means "self-production" in Greek, which is exactly what Seth glosses it as in the parenthetical.

In the passage, Seth is using this idea to make a specific point in his larger argument: even a single neuron isn't a passive component executing a fixed function, the way a transistor or a logic gate is. Even a single neuron is a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence. The parenthetical then names this self-maintaining activity — autopoiesis — and stakes out a claim: Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.

This matters for the essay's broader argument because it's one of the reasons Seth thinks brains resist the brain-as-computer metaphor. A standard computer chip doesn't need to constantly regenerate itself to keep functioning — its hardware is inert and stable, separate from whatever software runs on it. If autopoiesis is central to what a neuron *is*, then you can't cleanly peel apart "what the brain does" (computation) from "what the brain is made of" (biological matter), which is precisely the separation that makes the computer metaphor work. That's the move he's building toward in the surrounding paragraphs, where he argues brains have no good reason to expect such a clean separation between software and hardware the way computers do.

answers.asked: What does "autopoiesis" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
"Autopoiesis" is the article's term for a living thing's constant work of maintaining and regenerating its own material basis — even a single neuron is described as "busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence," and Seth glosses the word itself: "This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for 'self-production.' Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems" [spya-cf8rt8].

It matters to the argument in two places. First, in the "brains are not computers" section, autopoiesis is evidence that a brain's material stuff isn't separable from what it does — you can't split it into interchangeable "software" and "hardware" the way you can with a digital computer, which is the basis for Seth's whole case against computational functionalism (the claim that the right computation is enough for consciousness) [spya-b0086e spya-cf8rt8 spya-zw2m7u].

Second, it does heavier work later, in the "Life Matters" argument. There Seth tries to connect the brain's constant prediction-error-minimizing (its best-guessing about the world and body) to this same self-producing, autopoietic character of living material: "A mathematical line can be drawn directly from the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material all the way to the Bayesian best-guessing that underpins our perceptual experiences of the world and of the self" [spya-vys3vj]. That's the pivot from "brains aren't computers" to the stronger, more speculative claim that being alive — not just information processing — may be necessary for consciousness [spya-da9tvt spya-pfkhtt].

My inference is that autopoiesis is doing double duty in the piece: it's the concrete biological detail that makes "brains are not Turing machines" plausible, and it's also the conceptual bridge Seth needs to get from that negative claim to his positive, more speculative one (biological naturalism) — which he himself flags as a minority position he can't fully prove [spya-hj5y6s spya-qu7j89].
